into life in the US.

taken for renewal of the same.

1. Leave granted.
2. The  appellant  has  preferred  the  present  appeal
aggrieved  by  the  impugned  judgment  dated  30.09.2024
passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Karnataka  in  RFA
No.392/2023, whereby, the suit was decreed in favour of
the respondent, who is the plaintiff.  Vide the impugned
order,  the  judgment  rendered  by  the  Trial  Court,
dismissing the suit for permanent injunction was set
aside.  Additionally, the Trial Court had granted the
relief  of  possession  in  favour  of  the  appellant-
defendant qua the suit schedule property and directed
the respondent-plaintiff to handover vacant possession
of the same.  The same was reversed by the High Court.
Aggrieved, the appellant is before this Court.   
3. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
appellant  and  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
6

## Page 54

respondent at length.
4. Upon hearing the submissions made at the Bar, it is
agreed that the matter will be disposed of in the
following terms -
(i) The  appellant-defendant  shall  pay  a  sum  of
Rs.25,00,000/-  (Rupees  Twenty  Five  Lakhs)  to  the
respondent-plaintiff by way of Demand Draft, within a
period of four weeks from the date of receipt of a copy
of this order.
(ii) Upon receipt of the said amount, the respondent-
plaintiff shall hand over the vacant possession of the
suit  property  to  the  appellant-defendant,  within  a
period of four months, thereafter.
(iii) In view of the agreed terms, all disputes and
pending proceedings, both civil and criminal in nature,
initiated  by  the  parties  and  their  family  members
against each other, shall stand terminated.  Further,
the parties shall not initiate any further proceedings
either civil or criminal in nature, against each other.

between the parties, the impugned judgment passed by the
High Court stands set aside.

Court, in the event of non-compliance of this order or
any of the terms of aforestated settlement.

3

Diwa Dandi Light House Holi Tekra, Valsad, Taluka & District:
Valsad, developed friendship with me through my Instagram ID, and
with the intention of establishing physical relations, gave me a
promise of marriage, took me to Parnera Hill in Valsad and to other
different places, established physical relations repeatedly, and
upon refusing to marry, has committed the offense. Therefore, this
is my formal complaint. My witnesses are those mentioned in the

5. Thus,  it  appears  on  plain  reading  of  the  First
Information Report that the appellant and the Respondent No.2
were in a relationship past almost six years. However, the
allegations levelled by the Respondent No.2 are that she
maintained physical relations with the appellant relying upon
the promise which was given by the appellant that he would
marry her. This is the sum and substance of the accusation. 
6. Having  heard  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
parties and having gone through the materials on record, the
only question that falls for our consideration is whether the
High Court committed any error in passing the impugned Order. 
7. The issue now stands squarely covered by an Order passed
by a coordinate Bench in the case of “Kunal Rameshbhai Kalyani
versus State of Gujarat and Another”  Reported in 2026 SCC Online
SC 1818.
8. The relevant observations made therein applicable to the
facts of the present case are as under: 
“3.  The  High  Court  while  declining  the  prayer  for  quashing
specifically referred to the judgment of this Court in Deepak Gulati
v. State of Haryana (2013) 7 SCC 675; (2013) 3 SCC (Crl) 660 of
which paragraph 24 is extracted hereunder :

## Page 85

4
“24. Hence, it is evident that there must be adequate evidence
to show that at the relevant time i.e. at the initial stage
itself, the accused had no intention whatsoever, of keeping his
promise  to  marry  the  victim.  There  may,  of  course,  be
circumstances, when a person having the best of intentions is
unable  to  marry  the  victim  owing  to  various  unavoidable
circumstances. The “failure to keep a promise made with respect
to a future uncertain date, due to reasons that are not very
clear from the evidence available, does not always amount to
misconception of fact. In order to come within the meaning of
the  term  “misconception  of  fact”,  the  fact  must  have  an
immediate relevance”. Section 90 IPC cannot be called into aid
in such a situation, to pardon the act of a girl in entirety,
and fasten criminal liability on the other, unless the court is
assured of the fact that from the very beginning, the accused
had never really intended to marry her.” 
4. Under the IPC, the false promise of marriage was prosecuted under
Section 375 read with Section 90. Therein the requirement was to find
that the consent, if at all coming out from the facts, was tainted
insofar as the victim having been led to believe a promise of
marriage and physical relations having been permitted only on the
belief that the promise will be complied with; which the promisor
even at the time of giving such promise had no intention to comply
with. It was held in the aforesaid decision that misconception of
fact cannot be alleged if the promise is made with good intention and
later for unavoidable circumstances, the person is forced to resile
from the aforesaid promise. The BNS by incorporating Section 69
brought  in  a  separate  offence  carving  out  the  fraudulent  and
deceitful conduct as spoken of therein from the grave offence of
rape, while at the same time providing a penalty for the deceptive
conduct alleged therein. The word employed “deceitful means or by
making a promise to marry to a woman without any intention of
fulfilling the same” brings in the same rigor of the promise having
been given with an intention of never being fulfilled, which is the
deceitful conduct sought to be punished.
5. In the present case, the FIR has been extracted by the High Court
and it clearly indicates that the appellant and the complainant came
into contact through a digital platform and a friendship developed
between them, which later became a love affair. It is also stated in
the complaint that the appellant communicated his desire to marry the
complainant on the first physical meeting. The complainant is said to
have succumbed to his entreaties and allowed sexual intercourse. This
was on 12.02.2024 and again in April 2024, the victim is said to have
stayed in a hotel for two days with the appellant. The statements
made in the complaint clearly indicate a consensual relationship and
we do not find anything to find a deceitful conduct, of, the
appellant having induced the complainant into sexual intercourse,
which she succumbed to only on the promise to marry. Here we
reiterate that on the first occasion when they met, the complainant
succumbed to the appellant’s entreaties, is the specific statement
made without even stating that it was on the promise to marry that
physical relationship was permitted.”

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant, Laxmi Ray, is the complainant in P.S. Case/First
Information  Report  (FIR)  No.  154/2025  dated  26.05.2025
registered with Police Station – Khariar, District – Nuapada,
Odisha, for offences punishable under Sections 296, 3(5),
308(2) and 351(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.  The
said P.S. Case/FIR was registered by her alleging that the
accused/respondent Nos. 2 to 4 came to her workplace on
15.05.2025 and demanded money by threatening to defame her.
3. The accused/respondent Nos. 2 to 4 approached the High Court of
Odisha at Cuttack seeking anticipatory bail in relation to the
aforestated FIR by way of ABLAPL No. 7215/2025. The said
application was disposed of by the High Court, vide order dated
Crl.As. @ SLP(Crl.) Nos. 10077/2026 etc.     1

## Page 97

05.08.2025, wherein the High Court noted that the accused had
criminal  antecedents  of  a  similar  nature  and  expressed
disinclination to entertain their application for grant of
pre-arrest bail.  
4. Surprisingly, having stated so, the High Court proceeded to
direct the accused/respondent Nos. 2 to 4 to surrender before
the  learned  Judicial  Magistrate  First  Class1,  Khariar,  in
connection with the said case within one month and in the event
of their surrendering and filing a motion for bail, the learned
JMFC was directed to consider the same on merits during the
first hour of that day. The High Court further directed that,
in the event of rejection of the prayer for bail by the learned
JMFC, the accused would be at liberty to move the higher forum
for grant of bail during the second hour on the same day.  Not
stopping short at that, the High Court also directed the higher
forum to make an endeavour to dispose of the bail application
filed by the accused on the same day. The Case Diary was
directed to be made available to the concerned Courts to
facilitate disposal of the bail applications of the accused and
the learned JMFC was called upon to transmit the case record to
the higher forum at the earliest in the event of rejection of
the bail application filed by the accused.
5. Acting upon these directions of the High Court, the accused
approached the learned JMFC offering to surrender and seeking
bail by way of their petition in C.T. Case No. 153/2025.
1  “JMFC”, for short
Crl.As. @ SLP(Crl.) Nos. 10077/2026 etc.     2

## Page 98

However, the learned JMFC rejected their bail petition by way
of his order dated 16.12.2025.  
6. Taking a cue from the directions of the High Court, the accused
then filed BLAPL No. 36/2025 before the learned Additional
District and Sessions Judge2, Khariar, seeking bail in relation
to the aforestated FIR.  The learned ADSJ allowed the bail
application by way of order dated 16.12.2025.  
7. The appellant, Laxmi Ray, filed the appeal arising out of
SLP(Crl.) No. 10077/2026, assailing the order dated 05.08.2025
passed by the High Court, rejecting the anticipatory bail
application filed by the accused but, in effect, opening the
door for them to be granted regular bail. She, thereafter,
filed the appeal arising out of SLP(Crl.) No. 13443/2026,
challenging the order dated 16.12.2025 of the learned ADSJ in
BLAPL No. 36/2025, granting regular bail to the accused.
8. We may note, at this stage, that the learned ADSJ referred to
the order passed by the High Court on 05.08.2025 and opined
that, though the accused had criminal antecedents, they were
entitled to draw parity with a co-accused, who had already been
released on bail.  The learned ADSJ further noted that the
accused were ready to cooperate during the investigation as
well as the trial and, accordingly, granted them relief.
9. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties, we are of the
opinion that the matter on hand beseeches interference by this
Court.  Having arrived at the conclusion that the accused were
2  “ADSJ”, for short
Crl.As. @ SLP(Crl.) Nos. 10077/2026 etc.     3

## Page 99

not entitled to grant of anticipatory bail, it was not for the
High Court to then foretell the future course of action to be
undertaken by them and issue directions in that regard.  Not
only did the High Court undertake such an exercise, but also
fixed the time frame within which their application for relief
to be filed by them had to be considered.  In effect, the High
Court left no discretion for either the learned JMFC or the
learned ADSJ thereafter to independently assess the case with
proper application of mind.  That discretion stood curtailed by
the positive directions of the High Court, which just stopped
short of directing grant of bail straightaway to the accused.
The directions of the High Court, therefore, exceeded the
jurisdiction that the High Court was exercising in the context
of the accused’s anticipatory bail application.
10.  We are, therefore, of the opinion that the order dated
05.08.2025 passed by the High Court in ABLAPL No. 7215/2015 was
wholly unsustainable and is liable to be set aside for the
aforestated reasons.  Further, as the accused/respondent Nos. 2
to 4 deemed it appropriate to act upon the directions of the
High Court and secured relief from the learned ADSJ, the said
order also cannot be sustained, as the foundation thereof was
directions of the High Court.  That order is also liable to be
set aside.  
11. Both the appeals are, accordingly, allowed, setting aside the
order dated 05.08.2025 passed by the High Court and the order
dated 16.12.2025 passed by the learned ADSJ. 
Crl.As. @ SLP(Crl.) Nos. 10077/2026 etc.     4

## Page 100

12. The accused/respondent Nos. 2 to 4 would, however, be at
liberty  to  surrender  and  seek  regular  bail  before  the
appropriate forum in accordance with law.  Any such application
filed by them shall be considered on its own merits and in
accordance with law, uninfluenced by the earlier trajectory of
events and the present order.
Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

family. However, there is a request at the end of Supriya that on
17.12.2026, the school of Ananya is to celebrate sports day and
before leaving India, Ananya would like to participate in the
sports day on 17.12.2026. We permit Supriya and Ananya to stay back
in India till 17.12.2026. Sanil can fly down thereafter any time
and return to the USA with the family.
6. We are further informed that Ananya is to celebrate her
birthday on 14.12.2026. If that be so, Sanil may fly down one or
two days before Ananya’s birthday, celebrate the birthday on
14.12.2026, attend the sports day at her school and then fix one
date to fly back to the USA.
7. In any case, according to Ms. Diwan, Sanil will be arriving on
06.11.2026 for a period of six days. During that period, Sanil can
always meet Supriya and Ananya and spend good time with them. If
Supriya wants to visit India with Ananya to meet her parents, it is
always open for her to sort it out with Sanil. We are sure that in
this regard Sanil should not have any serious objection. However,
we may only say that the visit to India should not be frequent.
5

## Page 108

wife. We are sure that both together will plan their life further.

1. IA No. 277383/2026 is allowed.

3. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
4. This appeal impugns judgment and order of the
High  Court  of  Gujarat  at  Ahmedabad  dated
19.06.2026 whereby regular bail prayer of the
appellant in connection with FIR being CR No.
11205032210048  of  2021,  registered  at  P.S.
Mundra, Kutch, has been rejected.
5. At  the outset,  learned counsel  for the
appellant submits that this is a case where the
appellant has suffered incarceration of over 5
years pending trial. Besides, the prosecution
1

## Page 110

case relates to custodial torture/ beating of
two accused which resulted in their death. The
argument is that the appellant is not one of
those accused in whose custody the deceased
were  placed  at  the  time  when  they  were
assaulted; besides from the statement of PW-11,
an  injured  witness,  it  appears,  Jaydevsinh
Jhala, Shaktisinh Gohil, Ashok Kannad, Gafurji
Piraji  Thakor,  Kapilbhai  Amrutbhai  Desai,
Shambhu Devraj Ahir and Viral Joshi were the
ones who were beating the accused through the
night. It has been submitted that amongst those
accused, Shambhu Devraj Ahir and Viral Joshi
have been admitted to bail. In that backdrop,
it is submitted, the case of the appellant is
distinguishable from those in whose custody the
deceased were placed at the time when they were
assaulted and, therefore, having regard to the
fact  that  the  appellant  has  suffered
incarceration of over five years pending trial,
he is entitled to bail. 
6. The  learned  counsels  representing  the
respondent-State and the de-facto Complainant
have opposed the prayer for bail on the ground
2

## Page 111

that the allegation against the appellant is of
conspiracy to grab the property of the victim
and, therefore, it appears, at the instigation
of the appellant, the victims were assaulted.
However, the respondents have not been able to
dispute the fact that Shambhu Devraj Ahir and
Viral Joshi have been admitted to bail against
whom allegations of assaulting the victims are
there.
7. Upon considering the facts of the case and
the submissions of the learned counsel for the
parties, without expressing any opinion on the
merits thereof, having regard to the fact that
the appellant has suffered incarceration for a
period exceeding five years pending trial, and
it was not the appellant in whose custody the
victims were placed when they had received
injuries, we are of the view that the appellant
is entitled to be released on bail pending
trial, at this stage.
8.  Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The
order passed by the High Court rejecting the
regular bail prayer of the appellant is set
aside.

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties and have
perused the record.
3. The appellant was served a chargesheet and,
thereafter, the Summary Security Force Court found
him guilty. In consequence, appellant’s services were
dispensed with.
4. Aggrieved  by  the  order  of  dismissal  from
service, the appellant filed a writ petition before
the High Court at Calcutta which came to be dismissed
by a Single Judge vide order dated 08.12.2023.
5. Aggrieved by the order of the learned Single
Judge, an intra-court appeal was preferred before the
Division Bench of the High Court. The same was
1

## Page 116

registered as MAT  1623/2024. The Division Bench vide
judgment and order dated 04 September 2024 allowed
the appeal holding that the order of dismissal as
well as the appellate order were uninformed with
reasons and, therefore, they cannot be sustained. In
consequence,  those  order(s)  were  set  aside  and
parties were given liberty to proceed with the charge
as against the appellant from the stage prior to the
order of dismissal, or from any other stage prior
thereto, as may be deemed appropriate.
6. Aggrieved by the order of the Division Bench, a
Review Petition was filed by the Union of India (i.e.
the respondent herein). In the Review Petition, the
ground taken on behalf of the respondent was that the
Border Security Force Rules, 1969 (‘BSF Rules’) do
not contemplate recording of reasons and, therefore,
the view taken in the order dated 04.09.2024 was in
ignorance of the rule position and as such it was
amenable to a review. The Division Bench accepted the
aforesaid contention and without even recalling or
setting the earlier order dated 04.09.2024, by the
impugned  order,  straightaway  dismissed  the  writ
appeal by holding that no ground was made out to
2

## Page 117

interfere with the judgment and order of the learned
Single Judge.
7. Without addressing various grounds taken in
this appeal, the learned counsel for the appellant
submitted that the appropriate course for the High
Court while considering a review prayer was to first
recall or set aside the order under review and,
thereafter, hear the parties on merits of the appeal
in which the order under review was passed. It is
urged that while accepting the review, the High Court
has not adverted to all the grounds taken by the
appellant to assail the order of the learned Single
Judge  passed  in  the  writ  proceedings.  In  such
circumstances, it has been urged that the order
passed in review be set aside and the appeal i.e. MAT
1623/2024 be restored on the file of the High Court
for a fresh consideration on merits so that it may be
decided afresh after giving opportunity of hearing to
both sides.
8. Per  contra,  the  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-Union  submits  that  since  the  Division
Bench had allowed the intra-court appeal vide order
dated 04.09.2024 primarily on the ground that Summary
3

## Page 118

Security Force Court had not recorded reasons in
support of its order, and on review the High Court
found that it was not required to record reasons in
view of the provisions of the BSF Rules, there was no
requirement for the High Court to afford opportunity
of fresh hearing to the appellant on the intra-court
appeal.
9. However, the learned counsel for the appellant
could not demonstrate that before dismissing the writ
appeal the Division Bench of the High Court had
recalled its earlier order and, thereafter, heard the
parties on the writ appeal for final adjudication
thereof.
10. Having considered the rival submissions, we are
of the view that the High Court ought to have first
recalled or set aside the order under review upon
finding that the same was passed in ignorance of a
relevant provision of the BSF Rules and, thereafter,
it ought to have given opportunity to the parties to
address the court on the merits of the appeal before
affirming the judgment of the learned Single Judge
which was earlier set aside by the order under
review.
4

## Page 119

11. In such circumstances, we deem it appropriate
to set aside the order dated 23.04.2025 as well as
the earlier order dated 04.09.2024 and restore MAT
1623/2024 on the file of the High Court for a fresh
decision  on  merits  after  giving  opportunity  of
hearing to the parties/ their respective counsels. 
12. It is made clear that the High Court shall not
be  swayed  by  the  observations  contained  in  the
earlier orders dated 04.09.2024 and 23.04.2025 and
shall decide MAT 1623/2024 on its own merits.
13. The parties shall be at liberty to raise all
pleas, both on fact and law, as they may be advised
to take.
14. The present appeal and all pending applications
shall stand disposed of in the aforesaid terms.

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard the learned counsel for the parties.
3. The present appeals are filed against the impugned orders
dated 20.12.2013 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad, in Writ Petition No. 9680 of 2011
and Writ Petition No. 4940 of 2013. 
4. Respondent No. 06 is a cooperative society and was allotted
the licenses to run fair price shops bearing numbers 73, 77
and 78. It is the case of the appellant that the society, by
way of a resolution, granted the license for shop no. 77 to
him, in view of its inability to run it. 
5.  On  19th Jan  2004,  the  Deputy  Commissioner  (Supply),
Aurangabad, in case no. 2003/ACB/RP-357, passed an order
whereby the licenses of all the three shops were restored in
favour of respondent no. 06. A similar order was also passed

## Page 122

2
by the Minister (Food Civil Supply Department) on 18.08.2004.
Aggrieved by the same, the appellant herein filed a writ
petition in W.P. No. 9680 of 2011. 
6. On the other hand, on 23.01.2013, the Minister (Food, Civil
Supplies  and  Consumer  Protection)  passed  an  order,  in
revisional authority, restoring shop number 77 in favour of
the appellant. Aggrieved by the same, respondent No. 06 filed
a writ petition in W.P. No. 4940 of 2013. 
7. By the judgment and order dated 20.12.2013, the High Court
allowed Writ Petition No. 4940 of 2013 and set aside the order
dated 23.01.2013 that was passed in favour of the appellant.
The High Court also allowed the Writ Petition No. 9680 of 2011
and set aside the orders dated 19.01.2004 and 18.08.2004 that
were passed in favour of respondent No. 06. The High Court,
consequently, issued directions to the District Supply Officer
to follow due procedure and invite applications from eligible
persons to run the fair price shop. 
8. Aggrieved, both the appellant and respondent No. 06 filed
Special Leave Petitions before this court. The Special Leave
Petitions filed by respondent No. 06 in SLP (C) Nos. 2333 and
2879 of 2013 came to be dismissed vide order dated 08.09.2026
on account of non-prosecution and for not curing the defects.
9.   On perusal of the impugned decision of the High Court in
W.P. No. 9680 of 2011, we find that, although the dispute

## Page 123

3
pertained to Fair Price Shop No. 77, setting aside the orders
dated 19.01.2004 and 18.08.2004 affects Fair Price Shops Nos.
73 and 78, which are being run by the appellant-Society and
were not even the subject matter of the dispute. 
10. Coming to Fair Price Shop No. 77, it was given to the
appellant by respondent No. 06 when it was under liquidation.
Therefore, it was nothing but a temporary arrangement. In view
of the same, the license cannot be restored in favour of the
appellant. 
11. The High Court was wrong in setting aside the orders
dated 19.01.2004 and 18.08.2004, merely on the ground that the
appellant herein was not made a party to those proceedings.
Despite this being the case, we do not wish to interfere with
the impugned order as the Special Leave Petitions filed by
respondent No. 06, challenging the said findings, have already
been dismissed, as stated above. 
12. Coming to the impugned order passed in W.P. No. 4940 of
2013, the High Court has set aside the order dated 23.01.2013,
which restored the licence in favour of the appellant. The
High  Court  was  right  to  do  so,  given  the  serious
irregularities and discrepancies attributed to the appellant
herein. The High Court rightly held that the order dated
23.01.2013 was unreasoned. In view of the same, the order
requires no interference. 

## Page 124

4
13. Further, we are dealing with a case of licence, and no
right is vested in a licence. Even otherwise, the said licence
had been given to respondent no.06, which, in turn, had given
the same to the appellant during the interregnum when the
liquidation proceedings were pending.
14. In view of the above discussion and in view of the fact
that the Special Leave Petitions filed by respondent no. 06
have already been dismissed, the impugned orders require no
interference.
15. Accordingly, the appeals stand dismissed.
16. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.15873 of 2026)
STATE OF U.P.             ….APPELLANT(S) 
VERSUS
NAWAB SINGH YADAV              ….RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. Being aggrieved by order dated 16.12.2025 passed by
the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal
Miscellaneous Bail Application No.38636/2025, the State
of U.P. has preferred this appeal.
3. We  have  heard  Shri  S.V.  Raju,  learned  A.S.G.
appearing  for  the  appellant/State  of  U.P.  and  Shri
Shailesh Madiyal,  learned senior counsel appearing for
the  respondent/accused  and  perused  the  material  on
record.
4. At the outset, learned A.S.G. pointed out that the
respondent/accused  has  been  convicted  in  respect  of
another offence and is undergoing sentence of eight years
1

## Page 134

and has completed hardly one year of sentence. However,
in  the  instant  case,  having  regard  to  criminal
antecedents of the respondent which are also noted by the
High Court in the impugned order, namely, sixteen cases
of acquittal or discharge and bail being granted to the
accused in as many as ten cases and the present offence
would totally make twenty six antecedents and this is the
twenty seventh case.  Thus, the High Court ought to have
been cautious rather than citing the aforesaid instances
as a ground for grant of bail in the present case. He
also submitted that while in the earlier portion of the
order,  the  High  Court  declined  to  go  into  the
consideration of Section 19(4) of the U.P. Gangster and
Anti Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986 (for short,
“the Act”) but in the reasoning portion, the High Court
has stated that Section 19(4) of the Act has also been
taken  into  consideration  and  without  expressing  any
opinion on the merits of the case has granted the relief
of bail. He submitted that the invocation of the Act in
the instant case vis-à-vis the respondent/accused herein
is just and proper and hence bearing in mind the totality
of the facts and circumstances, this is a fit case where
the High Court ought to have declined grant of bail. On
2

## Page 135

the  other  hand,  the  High  Court  has  taken  into
consideration the totality of the facts and circumstances
and  has  granted  the  relief  of  bail.  He  therefore,
submitted that the impugned order may be set aside and
the appeal may be allowed.
5. Per  contra ,  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
respondent/accused  vehemently  contended  that  the  High
Court is justified in granting the relief of bail to the
appellant herein. Firstly, the invocation of the Act vis-
à-vis the appellant herein is not just and proper. Even
otherwise, the High Court has taken note of the fact that
the respondent herein has been granted bail in as many as
ten cases and has been acquitted or discharged in as many
as  sixteen  cases;  that  the  appellant/State  has  the
propensity of invoking the Act against the very same
persons without there being any rhyme or reason, the
present case is one such instance.  The High Court has
noted this aspect of the matter and has rightly granted
relief  to  the  appellant.  He  further  submitted  that
another co-accused Veerpal @ Nilu was granted bail by the
High Court and this Court vide order dated 17.08.2026
passed in SLP (Crl.) D. No.26801/2026 has dismissed the
3

## Page 136

Special Leave Petition.  Hence, on the principle of
parity the impugned order may not be interfered with.
6.  In  response  to  this  submission,  learned  A.S.G
contended that Veerpal @ Nilu is only a member of the
Gang whereas the respondent herein is the leader of the
Gang and therefore, the principle of parity cannot at all
be invoked in the present case and hence the appeal may
be allowed.
7. We have considered the arguments advanced at the Bar
and the material on record as well as the reasoning
adopted by the High Court in granting relief.
8. On a consideration of the impugned order, we find that
the order suffers from contraction and infirmity inasmuch
as in the first instance the High Court has stated that
it will not consider the controversy from the point of
view of Section 19(4) of the Act but in the operative
portion of the impugned Judgment of the High Court has
stated that the such provision has also been taken into
consideration  and  the  respondent  is  entitled  to  the
relief  of  bail.  The  criminal  antecedents  of  the
respondent/accused,  namely,  sixteen  cases  of  the
acquittal or discharge and ten cases where a bail has
4

## Page 137

been granted to him has been considered to be a positive
and affirmative aspect of the case and therefore, we find
that the said perception or the High Court is wholly
erroneous. The criminal antecedents of the accused ought
to  have  cautioned  the  High  Court  while  considering
whether the respondent was entitled to the relief of
bail. We find that the High Court has mis-directed itself
while  granting  the  relief  of  bail  to  the
respondent/accused in the instant case. Hence, we find it
just and proper to set aside the impugned order and allow
the appeal.  Consequently, the bail granted by the High
Court on 16.12.2025 stands cancelled.
9. We note that the respondent/accused is in jail as a
convict undergoing sentence.  However, this order may be
noted by the competent authorities. 
The appeal is accordingly allowed.

IA Nos.55920/2026 and 55922/2026 in Crl.A. Diary
No.4102/2026  and  IA  Nos.126927/2026  and
126928/2026 in Crl.A. No.2346/2026:
1. Heard. Admit. Delay condoned. 
2. The appellants who came to be tried for the offence
punishable under Sections 341, 294(b), 302, 506(2) of the
Indian  Penal  Code,  1860  came  to  be  acquitted  vide
judgment  dated  02.03.2022  and  the  said  finding  of
acquittal  came  to  be  reversed  by  the  High  Court  on
25.10.2025 in Criminal Appeal (MD) No.334/2022. Hence,
these appeals.
2

## Page 141

3. The case of the prosecution was that on 25.02.2015
that  about  08:15  to 09:15  hours  at  Thatchanallur  area,
near Galaxy Hospital, Palayamkottai, Tirunelveli - District,
T amil Nadu, the accused restrained Ponniah – the deceased
after dragging him out of his auto, abused him in filthy
language and murdered him by inflicting sickle injuries on
neck, head, chest and left hand causing his instantaneous
death and thereafter, fled from the scene. The trial court,
upon  appreciation  of  the  evidence  tendered  by  the
prosecution, by its judgment dated 02.03.2022, as noted
hereinabove, acquitted all the accused on the ground that
the  eyewitnesses,  namely,  PW-1,  PW-3  and  PW-4,  were
unreliable, being interested witnesses, and their presence
at the scene of occurrence as well as their version of the
incident were doubtful. The trial court also found material
contradictions  in  the  prosecution  case  regarding  the
manner  of  assault,  the  role  attributed  to  each  of  the
accused  and  the  sequence  of  events,  thereby  creating
serious  doubts  about  the  prosecution  case,  apart  from
other grounds assigned in its judgment.
3

## Page 142

4. The  complainant,  being  aggrieved  by  the  said
judgment of acquittal, filed an appeal before the Madurai
Bench of the Madras High Court and on re-appreciation of
the evidence, the High Court found that the testimonies of
PW-1, PW-3 and PW-4 were reliable eye-witnesses and held
that minor contradictions  did  not affect the  core  of  the
prosecution case. It was also noticed by the High Court
under  the  impugned  judgment  that  the  weapons  were
recovered  based  on  the  disclosure  statement  of  the
accused  and  same  was  accepted  as  a  corroboratory
evidence  connecting  them  to  the  offence.  Hence,
appellants,  came  to  be  convicted  and  sentenced  to  life
imprisonment. In these appeals, prayer for grant of bail by
suspension of sentence is sought for.
5. As could be seen from the records, the High Court
reversed the detailed reasoning of acquittal.  However, it
would suffice to state at this stage that High Court has not
recorded  finding  as  to  how  the  trial  court’s  view  was
perverse and it is not a plausible view. In the process of re-
appreciation of evidence, the material inconsistency that
4

## Page 143

has been brought to the forefront by the learned Sessions
Judge which undermines the case of the prosecution has
not  been  re-appreciated  as  could  be  seen  from  the
impugned  judgment.  However,  we  make  it  clear  at this
juncture itself that this view is for the limited purpose of
examining the prayer for suspension of sentence and grant
of bail only.
6. Apart from the aforesaid facts, it would also emerge
from the records that accused persons were on bail during
trial and only after being convicted by the appellate court,
they  have  surrendered  and  they  are  undergoing  the
sentence. There being no any untoward incident that has
occurred being attributable to appellants while the trial was
going on or in other words, the conditions of the bail having
not  been  violated,  we  are  of  the  considered  view  that
appellants  are  entitled  for  suspension  of  sentence  and
accordingly, the sentence imposed in Criminal Appeal (MD)
No.334/2022  by  the  Madras  High  Court,  Madurai  Bench
vide its judgment dated 25.10.2025 stands suspended and
appellants are ordered to be released on bail on such terms
5

## Page 144

and conditions as the jurisdictional Sessions Court deems
fit to impose. Accordingly, the applications are allowed.
7. Hearing is ordered to be expedited.
8. Registry to secure the trial court records. On receipt
of  the  same,  the  soft  copies  shall  be  furnished  to  the
learned respective counsels including the learned counsel
appearing for the State.
9. List the appeals on 03.12.2026.

WRIT PETITION(S)(CIVIL)  NO(S).  885/2025
MAHUA MOITRA                                        …PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ANR.                             …RESPONDENT(S)
 
O R D E R
This Writ Petition has been filed by an elected Member of
Parliament from Krishnanagar Lok Sabha constituency in West
Bengal seeking the following reliefs:
“a. Issue a Writ in the nature of Mandamus or any
other  Writ/Orders/Directions  to  the  Securities
and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to mandate
full  public  disclosure  of  Ultimate  Beneficial
Owners (UBO’s), Last Natural Persons (LNPs) And
Portfolio of Alternative Investment Funds (AIF’s),
Foreign  Portfolio  Investors  (FPI’s)  and  their
intermediaries in India.
b. Pass any other or further orders as this Hon’ble
Court may deem fit and proper in the facts and
circumstances of the case.”
1

## Page 146

2. An application was filed during the pendency of this Writ
Petition seeking amendment to the prayer column and to bring on
record the reply of the Securities and Exchange Board of India
(“SEBI” for short) dated September 19, 2025, a copy of which has
been produced in the amended Writ Petition as Annexure (P-3).
3. We have heard learned counsel, Shri Prashant Bhushan for
the petitioner and learned Solicitor General for Union of India and
SEBI/respondent Nos.1 and 2 respectively at length. We have
also perused the contents of the memorandum of Writ Petition
leading up to the aforesaid prayers.
4. We take note of prayer-“A” of the Writ Petition. The petitioner
is seeking a direction by way of a writ of mandamus to SEBI to
make public disclosure of Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBO’s),
Last  Natural  Persons  (LNPs)  and  Portfolio  of  Alternative
Investment Funds (AIF’s), Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI’s) and
their intermediaries in India. As we have noted, in the amended
Writ Petition, a copy of the reply dated 19.09.2025 issued to the
petitioner  by  SEBI  has  stated  in  the  context  of  the  aforesaid
prayer in paragraph 6 as under:
2

## Page 147

“6. The AIF Regulations and FPI Regulations do not
mandate public disclosure of entity-wise investments.
However, disclosures of investments by every AIF/FPI
are in fact made to SEBI/Custodians which enable
regulation,  detailed  investigation  when
circumstances  so  warrant  and  support  policy
formulation. Importantly, disclosures of investments
on  an  aggregate  basis  are  made  category-wise,
sector-wise  etc.  which  enable  public  and  investor
awareness  of  investments  made  by  the  AIF/FPI
industry. Moreover, in accordance with the mandate
in  the  SEBI  (Listing  Obligations  and  Disclosure
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 which is applicable
to all shareholders owning more than 1% of listed
entities, investments held in a listed entity by an AIF
or FPI is also disclosed. Similarly, under the SEBI
(Substantial  Acquisition  of  Shares  and  Takeovers)
Regulations,  2011,  shares  held  by  all  investors
including AIFs and FPIs beyond specified thresholds
are disclosed on a periodic basis. The compiled list of
periodic/event  based  disclosures  of  investments
made to SEBI/Custodians as well as those which are
publicly disclosed are recorded.”
5. On a reading of the same, we find that presently there is no
legal  framework  to  make  a  public  disclosure  of  entity-wise
investments.  However,  disclosures  of  investments  by  every
AIF/FPI are in fact made to SEBI, the custodians, which enable
regulations to be made as well as detailed investigation when
warranted.
3

## Page 148

6. On a reading of the reply of SEBI, we find there is no legal
framework or any regulatory framework as such in force which
mandates public disclosure as sought for by the petitioner herein
in prayer-“A”. In this writ petition filed under Article 32 of the
Constitution  of  India,  the  petitioner  is  seeking  such  a  public
disclosure even in the absence of such a regulatory framework. 
7. Having heard learned counsel for the petitioner and learned
Solicitor General for respondent Nos.1 and 2, we find that in
exercise of our jurisdiction under Article 32 of the Constitution of
India, such a prayer cannot be granted for the reason that the full
public disclosure as sought for by the petitioner herein would
require the creation of a legal framework of regulations in the first
instance. In the absence of such a legal framework of regulations,
this  Court  cannot  direct  a  full  public  disclosure  of  Ultimate
Beneficial Owners(UBO’s). In the above circumstances, we find
that the prayers sought for by the petitioner herein cannot be
granted by this Court. The Writ Petition is accordingly liable to be
disposed of.
4

## Page 149

8. We say so for the reason that it is ultimately for the Union of
India and second respondent-SEBI to put in place a framework
under which such a disclosure could be made. In the absence of
any such framework, this Court cannot exercise its discretion and
direct or issue a Writ of mandamus to direct SEBI to make a full
public disclosure. That would be a case of putting the cart before
the horse.
9. We opine that in a petition  filed under Article 32 of the
Constitution, this Court may not issue directions touching upon
matters  of  policy  or  governance  and  issue  directions  in  the
absence  of  a  legislative  or  regulatory  framework.  However,  in
exceptional  cases,  this  Court,  in  exercise  of  its  discretion  or
powers under Article 142 of the Constitution, may do so. But in
the instant case, we do not find the need to issue such directions.
10. We however, opine that it is for the respondents herein to
consider the matter in their wisdom in light of the discussions
that have been made in the Court in the interest of investors in
corporate and other entities.
5

## Page 150

11. The Writ Petition is disposed of in aforesaid terms.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Madhya
Pradesh.
3. Appellant has been convicted by the Trial Court under
Sections 333/34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short,
‘IPC’) and sentenced to undergo Rigorous Imprisonment (for
short,  ‘R.I.’)  for  07  years  and  to  pay  a  fine  of
Rs.3,000/- with a default stipulation.
4. Aggrieved by the aforesaid conviction and sentence,
appellant has preferred an appeal before the High Court of
Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur (briefly ‘the High Court’
hereinafter), which has been registered as CRA No.7775 of
2025. In the aforesaid appeal, appellant had preferred an
Interlocutory Application for suspension of sentence and
1

## Page 157

grant of bail.
5. By the impugned order dated 02.02.2026, the High
Court rejected the aforesaid application of the appellant.
6. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that two of
the  co-convicts  have  been  granted  the  benefit  of
suspension  of  sentence  and  bail  by  the  High  Court.
Referring to the incident for which the appellant has been
convicted, he submits that it arose out of altercation
during Holi celebrations. The injured is a policeman who
suffered fracture on his little finger of the left hand.
7. On  the  other  hand,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State of Madhya Pradesh submits that till date,
appellant  has  undergone  about  01  year  03  months  of
incarceration out of the total sentence of 07 years. At
this stage, appellant may not be enlarged on bail. He
further submits that the charge against the appellant was
of assaulting a policeman on duty, which has been proved.
8. Having regard to the rival submissions made at the
Bar and on due consideration, we are of the view that a
case for suspension of sentence and grant of bail is made
out. We are further fortified in taking this view by the
fact that the pending criminal appeal before the High
Court is of the year 2025 and there is no possibility of
hearing of the appeal in the near future.
9. That being the position, t he impugned order dated
02.02.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
10. Consequently, we suspend the sentence and direct that
2

the appellant shall released on bail forthwith on usual
terms and conditions.
11. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(s).           OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO(s). 17080-17081/2026)
K. DHARMARAJAN & ORS.      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF TAMIL NADU & ORS.     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellants
namely K. Dharamarajan, D. Chellammal, Nathiya and D.
Baviya; learned counsel for Respondent No.1-State of Tamil
Nadu; and learned counsel for Respondent No.2- de-facto
complainant.
3. Appellants had moved for anticipatory bail before the
High Court of Judicature at Madras, Madurai Bench (briefly
‘the High Court’ hereinafter) as they were named as
accused in Crime No.06/2022 lodged by the complainant
before  the  Police  Station-  Tiruppathur,  District-
Sivagangai, Tamil Nadu under Sections 498A, 342 and 506(1)
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) read
with Sections 4 and 6 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.
1

## Page 162

4. Vide the order dated 07.10.2022, the High Court
granted anticipatory bail to the appellants, subject to
certain conditions. One of the conditions mentioned as
clause (b) of paragraph 8 reads as follows:
“[b] the husband of the defacto complainant/A1
shall come down to India within six months from
today, so as to settle the dispute between the
parties  amicably.  In  the  meanwhile,  A1  is
directed to pay a sum of Rs.20,000/- (Rupees
Twenty Thousand only) per month towards interim
maintenance in the defacto complainant’s account,
on the first week of every English Calendar
month, till the same is modified by any of the
proceedings of the Court of law.”
5. It  is  stated  that  A-1  is  the  husband  of  the
complainant, who is residing abroad and he was not one of
the petitioners who had sought anticipatory bail before
the High Court. It was only the appellants herein who were
before the High Court.
6. With the allegation that the appellants did not
comply with the aforesaid condition, complainant moved the
High Court for cancellation of the anticipatory bail,
whereafter the High Court passed the impugned order dated
27.11.2025 rejecting the anticipatory bail granted to the
appellants  on  the  ground  that  the  husband  of  the
complainant  had  failed  to  return  to  India  and  pay
maintenance to the informant.
7. This Court vide order dated 24.08.2026 had issued
notice and in the meanwhile, stayed the impugned order
2

## Page 163

dated 27.11.2025, qua the appellants.
8. Learned counsel for Respondent No.1-State of Tamil
Nadu as well as learned counsel for Respondent No.2- de
facto complainant  vehemently  argued  that  it  was  the
appellants themselves who had given an assurance before
the  High  Court  that  A-1,  i.e.  the  husband  of  the
informant, would return to India and pay maintenance to
the complainant. It is because of their assurance that the
High Court had incorporated such a condition in the bail
order. Naturally when such aforesaid condition was not
complied  with,  the  High  Court  rightly  cancelled  the
anticipatory bail granted to the appellants.
9. Time and again, this Court has reiterated that while
considering the prayer of anticipatory bail of an accused,
the Court should not impose conditions like payment of
maintenance etc., for which there is a separate forum and
procedure. A process of bail or anticipatory bail cannot
be converted into a forum for grant of maintenance, more
so when A-1, i.e. the husband, was not a party before the
High Court. Further, appellants have no control over A-1
who resides abroad. If the husband does not come back to
India  and  pay  the  maintenance  to  the  complainant,
appellants cannot be held responsible for such conduct of
the husband.
10. That being the position, t he impugned order dated
27.11.2025 passed in Crl. M.P(MD). No.5078 of 2025 in
Crl.O.P(MD). No.18062 of 2022 by the High Court is set
3

## Page 164

aside to the extent of cancellation of anticipatory bail
granted to the appellants by the High Court.
11. We direct that the appellants, i.e. K. Dharamarajan,
D. Chellammal, Nathiya and D. Baviya, shall continue to
remain on pre-arrest bail, subject to the conditions
imposed by the High Court vide order dated 07.10.2022,
except clause (b), as aforesaid. However, appellants shall
appear before the Trial Court on the dates fixed.
12. The Criminal Appeals are, accordingly, allowed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

demonstrate any past criminal antecedent of the
appellant.
6. Having regard to the facts of the case, without
expressing  any  opinion  on  merits  of  the
prosecution case, we are of the view that the
appellant is entitled to be released on bail at
this stage.
7. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed.  The
order passed by the High Court rejecting the bail
prayer of the appellant is set aside.

K.V. SEETHARAMAN PRESIDENT OF

                                VERSUS
THE ASSISTANT COMMISSIONER H.R. 
AND C.E. ADMIN DEPT. & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing for the
appellant and the learned Senior counsel appearing for the
respondents. 
2. The appellant herein instituted a suit in the year 1988, for
declaration of the right to manage and administer the affairs
of  Sri  Venugopalswamy  Bajanaimadam  and  for  consequential
injunction, which was decreed by the Trial Court vide order
dated 18.09.1995. The High Court, vide order dated 16.12.2009,
in an appeal by the respondents reversed the findings of the
Trial  Court,  by  holding  that  the  suit  itself  was  not
maintainable in the absence of a declaration having been
obtained from the Deputy Commissioner under Section 63(a) of
the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act,

## Page 182

2
1959 (hereinafter 'the said Act').
3. In the present case, the short issue involved is, as to
whether the judgment and decree of the High Court in holding
that the suit is not maintainable is proper or not. 
4. While concurring with the High Court's conclusion, we are
inclined to hold that there is no need for incidental findings
on facts. In fact the appellant did invoke Section 63(a) of
the said Act, which was dismissed on default. Suffice it is to
state, that in view of the judgment of the High Court, there
is no bar for the appellant to invoke Section 63(a) of the
said Act once again, particularly, by taking note of the fact
that the earlier application was dismissed on default. 
5. In such view of the matter, we are inclined to grant six weeks
time to the appellant from the date of receipt of a copy of
this order to invoke Section 63(a) of the said Act. 
6. Such application being filed before the concerned authority
namely, Joint/Deputy Commissioner, shall be disposed of within
a period of three months thereafter. Till such time, status
quo as of today, shall be maintained by the parties.
7. We make it clear that the competent authority is directed to
decide the application on its own merits and in accordance
with the law, without being influenced by any of the findings
on merit rendered by the High Court in the impugned judgment. 
8. The appeal stands disposed of, in the aforesaid terms and with
aforementioned directions.

1. Leave granted. 
2. The appellant has been arraigned as an accused
and  seeks  regular  bail  in  connection  with
Criminal  Case  No.DGGI/INT/INTL/1053/2025-GrA
instituted by the Directorate General of GST
Intelligence, Jaipur Zonal Unit for the offences
punishable  under  Sections  132(1),(c),(f),(h),
(i) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act,
2017.
3. We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing for the appellant and the learned
Additional Solicitor General (ASG) appearing for
the respondent.
4. The learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
1

## Page 192

appellant has submitted that investigation is
completed qua the appellant and the chargesheet
has been filed.
5. The learned ASG appearing for the respondent
submitted that this Court has rejected the bail
application of the accused and the said person
has not yet surrendered even after expiry of the
time granted. Therefore, non-bailable warrant
has been issued against him.
6. We have perused the earlier order passed by this
Court  in  SLP  (Crl.)  No.10719/2026  dated
03.08.2026.  There  are  two  distinguishable
factors, we notice. Firstly, the said petition
has been dismissed primarily on the ground that
there are criminal antecedents. On a query,
learned  ASG  has  submitted  there  are  no
antecedents  pertaining  to  the  appellant.
Secondly, the said order has been passed on
03.08.2026, and therefore, three months have
elapsed thereafter. The maximum punishment that
can be imposed for the offence alleged is five
years. The appellant has already undergone about
nine months.
7. Taking  note  of  the  aforesaid  fact,  we  are
2

## Page 193

inclined to set aside the impugned order passed
by  the  High  Court,  and  grant  bail  to  the
appellant.

aside, and the appellant is granted regular
bail, subject to the terms and conditions that
may be imposed by the concerned Trial Court. 
9. The appeal is allowed, accordingly.

CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).        OF 2026
(@ SLP (C) NOS. 26717-26718 OF 2023)

                                VERSUS
ALI AJGAR & ANR.                                   Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present Civil Appeal by way of special leave arises out of
the order dated 28.08.2023 passed by the Tripura High Court in L.A.
Appeal No. 66 and 86 of 2023 whereby the High Court directed the
appellant to pay compensation for the rubber trees @  9,500/- per₹
tree and further directed solatium of twice of the amount and
interest @ 15% p.a.
3. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
4. Mr. Gaurav Agarwal, learned senior counsel appearing for the
appellant raised a neat point of law. He would submit that
acquisition in the present case arises out of the power invoked
under Section 81 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency
in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013
(hereinafter referred to as 'the Act'). The acquisition in this
1

## Page 197

C.A. Nos. @ SLP (C) NOS. 26717-26718 OF 2023
case related to taking temporary possession of land which comprised
of 400 rubber trees. Compensation in terms of acquisition under
Section 81 was determined by Land Acquisition Officer (LAO) on
06.01.2016 by granting  700 per tree. The said amount was enhanced₹
by Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Authority
(LARR) by order dated 01.12.2022. It was in such determination
itself that the difficulty arose, when the Authority proceeded
further and granted 100% solatium  over and above the compensation
payable towards the trees.  Specifically challenging the said grant
of solatium, the appellant filed LA Appeal No. 66 of 2023 before
the High Court. The question relating to legality and validity of
granting solatium was raised in the following terms:
"[13]  The  Learned  Court  has  erred  in  not
appreciating that the proceedings are related
to temporary acquisition of land under Section
81  of  the  Act,  2013  and  therefore,  100%
solatium cannot be imposed on the amount so
determined by the learned Authority. Learned
Authority failed to appreciate that present
case being of temporary acquisition interest
under Section 72 of the Act, 2013 cannot be
imposed  which  is  applicable  exclusively  in
cases of permanent acquisition of the land.
Learned  Authority  thus  erred  in  not
appreciating that interest under section 72 of
the Act is awarded in the course of and as a
part of permanent acquisition."
5. However, the High Court while enhancing the compensation to
 9,500/- per tree had not discussed about the order of LARR₹
granting  solatium.  Mr.  Gaurav  Agarwal  therefore  submits  that
judgment of the High Court, to the extent it grants solatium is not
sustainable in law. 
6. In the normal course, we would have either determined the
2

## Page 198

C.A. Nos. @ SLP (C) NOS. 26717-26718 OF 2023
issue raised by Mr. Gaurav Agarwal or even remanded the matter to
the High Court for fresh determination of this issue.  However, in
the said facts and circumstances of the case, as the respondent has
been contesting the matter since 2016, when the acquisition had
taken  place,  in  order  to  do  complete  justice,  we  deem  it
appropriate to dispose of the appeals by passing the following
order:
A. The Judgment and Order passed by the High Court and the LARR
to the extent they grant solatium are set aside. However, we direct
the appellant to grant 25% of the total amount payable, as
determined @  9,500/- per tree. The said amount will be ₹ ex-gratia
and is granted only in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the
case. The amount shall be deposited by the appellant before the
Executing Court within a period of eight weeks from today for
withdrawal by respondent(s). 
7. With these directions, the present proceedings stand closed
and the Civil Appeals stand disposed of.

the safe vault was opened prior to the commencement of
transactions of the branch, and the then Branch Manager
noticed shortage of Rs.24,12,326/-. However, no complaint
was lodged, nor was the matter brought to the notice of the
higher authorities.

noticing  the  discrepancy,  the  Branch  Manager  informed
about  the  shortage  of  the  cash  to  the  Head  Office  on
16.07.2026. Thereafter, it was referred for conducting an
inquiry on 22.07.2026 and complaint came to be lodged on
23.07.2026 by the Bank to the jurisdictional police station,
resulting in registration of FIR No. 371/2026 and appellant
along with the Branch Manager was arraigned as accused.

prejudice  the case of the prosecution. Hence, we desist

recorded who stated that Sanjay Yadav was tenant in the residence
of the deceased and on his asking for vacating the house, he was
not vacating the house, there was mutual dispute and animosity, as
a result of which on 22.1.2021 at about 9 am he had quarrel and
abusive hot talks with Yashoda Bai. The said suicide note was sent
to handwriting expert Raipur for examination which was returned
after scrutiny on some points which is to be sent again. Since in
the merg inquiry, as per the entire investigation conducted so far,
in the house constructed on the half portion of residence of
deceased Balvinder Singh, accused Sanjay Yadav was living on rent
with his family and on deceased demanding rent and for vacating the
house, there was dispute and animosity, Anusuiya Yadav wife of
Sanjay Yadav was working in the house of Akash Sharma in the past,
therefore, Akash Sharma was also in favour of them and was giving
them shelter for not vacating the house. Thus due to above dispute
in relation to the rented house the deceased out of torture
appeared to have committed suicide by hanging.
Hence upon the entire investigation in the matter and investigation
verification by me, offence under Section 306, 34 of IPG being
prima facie found against accused persons Sanjay Yadav and elder
sister-in-law Purnima Yadav and mother-in-law Yashoda Bai and
accomplice  Akash  Sharma  resident  of  Bazar  Mohalla  Ward  No.3
Katghora, the offence having been registered was taken up for
investigation. Copy of Merg Intimation No.11/2021 is annexed. As
per Untimely Death Information Register (Section 174 CrPC) Police
Station Katghora Dist. Korba CG Merg No. 11/21 the cause of death
is hanging, name and address of the deceased Balvinder Singh s/o
Late Dharam Singh Jat, aged 40 years. Bazar Mohalla Katghora Ward
No.3, date, time of incident 22.1.2021 in between 8 am and 10 am,
place of occurrence Bazar Mohalla Katghora house of the deceased,
date and time of information 22.1.21 at 12.00 o'clock, name of
informant Nirmala Rajput w/o Jaswant Singh Jat, aged 40 years,
resident of BankimongraQut. No.34/03, Police Station Bankimongra,
details - informant with her husband Jaswant Si.ngh appeared before
Police Station, lodged oral merg intimation that her husband has
three brothers, elder one is her husband and younger brother was
Balvinder Singh who was living at Bazar Mohalla, Katghora with
family and his wife is Tuli Kaur who had gone to her parental house
at Korba on 20.1.2021 in the evening due to quarrel with her
husband, her brother-in-law drives Auto and was habitual to liquor,
had given half of his house on rent, two days ago in the night her
sister-in-law (devrani) informed her over telephone from Korba that
there was quarrel between her husband and the tenant, therefore,
she came to her parental house with children, on which she came to
Katghora with her female acquaintance and went to the house of her
brother-in-law  alone  and saw that her brother-in-law had died due

## Page 223

3
to hanging in the room, seeing this she got scared and immediately
having rushed out informed the neighbourers at 11 o clock and after
informing the family members, has come to lodge the report. Upon
information,  having  registered  merg,  panchanama  proceeding
commenced, information is sent to SDM. Illegible signature in
English of Nirmala Rajput, illegible signature in English of
investigator on 22.1.21”
5. Thus, on plain reading of the First Information Report, it
appears that four persons have been named as accused. The appellant
before us viz. Akash Sharma is figures as Accused No.4 in the First
Information Report. It further appears that the three co-accused
were put to trial for the alleged offence. They came to be
acquitted vide the Judgment and Order dated 3rd October, 2024. The
appellant before us was not put to trial as some interim protection
was granted by this Court, as a result charge-sheet was not filed
against him, and therefore he could not be put to trial along with
the three co-accused.
6. It also appears from the materials on record that the deceased
left behind a suicide note. The suicide note reads thus: 
"I Balvinder Singh am giving a statement in my senses that I have
been forced to commit suicide by Akash Sharma and his friend
Purnima Yadav and Yashoda Bai, Sanjay Yadav who are close to me,
all of them are trying to kill me (unclear). After my death,
neither my brother will be given a shroud nor will he be buried. If
they give him a shroud or burial, my soul will not get peace.
1 Balvinder Singh having forced by Akash Sharma and my tenant, am
committing suicide because as long as my parents were alive,
everything was fine. After my parents died, these people took
advantage of handicapped people like us, meaning both husband and
wife are handicapped. These people are taking advantage of this and
1 am unclear). I Balvinder Singh is (unclear) in my senses that I
am dying under the pressure of others (unclear)”.
7. At the end of the trial, insofar as the three co-accused are
concerned,  the  Trial  Court  reached  the  conclusion  that  the
prosecution had failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond

## Page 224

4
reasonable doubt. To put it in other words, the Trial Court
recorded a categorical finding that even if all the allegations as
leveled are accepted to be true and even if whatever has been
stated in the suicide note is believed to be true, none of the
ingredients to constitute the offence of abetment of suicide could
be said to have been made out. In fact, the trial court disbelieved
the very execution of the suicide note by the deceased.
8. In such circumstances referred to above, we believe that
putting the appellant now to trial on the same set of evidence will
be an empty formality. 
9. In such circumstances, we allow this appeal. The criminal
proceedings against the appellant herein are hereby quashed. 
10. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

PUNEET RASTOGI      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF U.P. & ANR.       RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
and learned counsel for Respondent No.1-State of
Uttar  Pradesh.  None  has  appeared  on  behalf  of
Respondent No.2.
3. We  may  mention  that  following  orders  dated
17.09.2026  and  14.10.2026,  when  there  was  no
representation on behalf of Respondent No.2 despite
being served, we decided to proceed ex-parte against
her.
4. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 07.07.2026
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad,
Lucknow Bench (briefly ‘the High Court’ hereinafter),
rejecting the application filed by the appellant
under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973 (for short, ‘CrPC’) for quashing of Complaint
1

## Page 232

Case  No.107/2019  pending  before  the  Civil  Judge
(J.D)/FTC (Crime Against Women), Lucknow.
5. Appellant is the husband and Respondent No.2 is
the  wife.  Their  marriage  was  solemnized  on
18.04.2017.  Unfortunately,  differences  cropped  up
between them thereafter, leading to allegations of
violence by appellant against Respondent No.2. Though
an  endeavour  was  made  for  resolution  of  the
matrimonial  dispute  amicably,  the  same  was  not
successful.
6. On  01.02.2019,  Respondent  No.2  filed  an
application under Section 12 of the Protection of
Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 before the
Chief  Judicial  Magistrate,  Lucknow,  which  was
registered as Complaint Case No.107/2019 and assigned
to the Court of Civil Judge (J.D)/FTC (Crime Against
Women), Lucknow.
7. In the meanwhile, appellant instituted divorce
proceedings  against  Respondent  No.2,  being
Miscellaneous Case No.1103/2019 before the Court of
Additional Principal Judge, Court No.8, Family Court,
Lucknow.  Respondent  No.2  filed  Matrimonial  Suit
No.145/2025 under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage
Act, 1955 for restitution of conjugal rights.
2

## Page 233

8. By the judgment and order dated 01.03.2025, a
decree of divorce under Section 13 of the Hindu
Marriage Act, 1955 was granted. The suit preferred by
Respondent No.2 for restitution of conjugal rights
came to be rejected.
9. It is in this backdrop that when we look at the
impugned order of the High Court, we find that the
High Court has proceeded on the basis that there was
a judicial separation between the parties which did
not put an end to the marriage; hence the domestic
relation continued between the husband and wife,
though they may not be actually living together.
Therefore, the allegation of domestic violence would
survive.
10. This finding of the High Court is contrary to the
record and cannot be sustained, in view of the fact
that the matrimonial bond between the husband and the
wife was severed by the decree of divorce dated
01.03.2025.
11. While we are inclined to quash the impugned order
dated 07.07.2026 passed by the High Court as well as
the Complaint Case No.107/2019, we are also of the
view that liberty should be granted to Respondent
No.2 to seek for alimony before the appropriate
3

## Page 234

forum, if she so chooses.
12. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order
dated 07.07.2026 passed by the High Court. We also
quash the Complaint Case No.107/2019 pending before
the Court of Civil Judge (J.D)/FTC (Crime Against
Women), Lucknow.
13. Subject  to  the  observations  made  above,  the
Criminal  Appeal  is  allowed,  with  liberty  to
Respondent No.2 as above.
14. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

## Page 271

2
SLP (CRL) No. 16881/2026
1. The present Special Leave Petition calls in question the order
dated 22.08.2023 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna in
Criminal Miscellaneous  Case No. 53684 of 2023, whereby , further
proceedings in POCSO Case No. 33 of 2022 arising out of Mahila P.S.
Case No. 19 of 2022, pending in the Court of Additional District
and Sessions Judge-VI-cum-Special Judge, POCSO Act, Buxar, Bihar
have been stayed.
2. The proceedings originate from FIR No. 19/2022 registered at
Mahila P.S., District Buxar, Bihar against the respondent No. 2-
accused for the offences punishable under  Sections 341, 323  and
354B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (hereinafter referred to as the
“IPC”) and Section 8 of the Protection of Children from Sexual
Offences Act, 2012 (hereinafter referred to as the “POCSO Act”).
3. On 28.05.2022, a charge sheet was filed by the Investigating
Officer against the respondent No. 2 and on 28.06.2022, the Special
Judge took cognizance  of the offences punishable under Sections
341, 323 and 354B of the IPC and Section 8 of the POCSO Act. On
31.08.2022, the respondent No. 2 was enlarged on bail.
4. On 06.05.2023, the Trial Court rejected an application filed
by the respondent No. 2 under Sections 91 and 311 Cr.P.C., seeking,
inter alia , production of CCTV footage and examination of the
Investigating Officer. The Trial Court recorded the following
findings:
" Heard the parties and perused the record. In this case,
the investigator concluded the investigation on April 30,
2022, and submitted a charge sheet on May 28, 2022. A
perusal of the records reveals that on April 16, 2022, an

## Page 272

3
SLP (CRL) No. 16881/2026
application was filed by the applicant/accused requesting
the court to order the investigator to submit the CCTV
footage to the court. A 32 GB pen drive was also submitted
by the accused/applicant along with the application dated
April 16, 2022, which the court forwarded to the SP, Buxar.
A perusal of the record reveals that in this case, charges
were framed by the court on 08.07.2022, after complying with
Section 207 of the CrPC. All witnesses in the case were
examined on various dates thereafter. Since all witnesses
except one have been examined at this stage of the trial,
the applicant/accused’s claim that complete compliance with
Section  207  of  the  CrPC  has  not  been  made  appears
unreasonable. A perusal of the record reveals that all the
materials for the investigation based on which the charge
sheet has been framed were provided to the applicant/accused
on 08.07.2022. At this stage of the trial, when only the
investigation remains to be conducted, it does not appear
justified  to  accept  the  applicant’s  application.  The
applicant/accused  has  filed  the  following  judgments  in
support of his application: 1. P. Ponnusamy v. State of
Tamil Nadu, (2022) 15 SCALE 230; and 2. P. Gopal Krishnan v.
State of Kerala & others, (2021) 1 SCC (Cri) 147. The
judgments passed on behalf of the applicant/accused are
applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present
case. It appears that the application filed on behalf of the
applicant/accused has been filed with the intention of
delaying  the  trial.  Therefore,  the  application  dated
12.01.2023 filed on behalf of the applicant/accused is
dismissed."
5.  This order was challenged by respondent No. 2 in Criminal
Miscellaneous  Case No. 53684 of 2023 and while issuing notice,
proceedings were stayed before the Trial Court. The stay remained
for over 3 years and 2 months.

## Page 273

4
SLP (CRL) No. 16881/2026
6. The de facto complainant is before us . We are of the opinion
that the High Court should expeditiously dispose of Criminal
Miscellaneous  Case  No.  53684  of  2023,  so  that  there  is  no
impediment in proceeding with the trial. Learned counsel for the
State and learned counsel for the respondent No. 2-accused are all
ad idem that the High Court proceedings should be disposed of
expeditiously. 
7. Considering that the offence involved is an offence under the
POCSO Act, it is all the more important that the trial is concluded
expeditiously. We are of the opinion that the High Court should
dispose of the Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 53684 of 2023 within
a period of four weeks from today.
8. Let a copy of this order be forwarded to the Registra r General
of the High Court of Judicature at Patna who may, who may on
receipt of the order place the same before the Hon'ble Chief
Justice of the High Court of Judicature at Patna for appropriate
directions.
9. With  the  directions  aforementioned,  this  Special  Leave
Petition is disposed of.
10. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

77, 79, 351(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
2. This Court, vide order dated 22.09.2026, granted
interim protection to the petitioner in the matter.
Pursuant thereto, the petitioner has appeared before the
Investigating  Officer  and  cooperated  with  the
investigation.  The  investigation  has  since  been
completed, and the charge-sheet has also been filed
before the competent court.
3. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
as well as the complainant submit that the petitioner has
not  furnished  the  requisite  passwords  and  access
2

## Page 288

credentials for his Cloud storage and Telegram account,
and express apprehension that the material collected on
his mobile phone may be circulated.
4. This Court after hearing learned counsel for the
parties and taking into consideration the fact that the
charge-sheet has already been filed and the petitioner
has joined the investigation, is of the opinion that the
interim  order  dated  22.09.2026  deserves  to  be  made
absolute.
5. Accordingly, interim order dated 22.09.2026 is
made absolute subject to the condition that petitioner
shall continue to co-operate with the investigation and
shall report as and when called upon to do so by the
Investigating Authority.
6. However, petitioner is directed to furnish all
necessary details, credentials, and passwords relating to
his Cloud ID, Telegram account, and other social media
platforms to the investigating Officer.
7. The petitioner shall abide by his undertaking
given before this Court that he shall not circulate or
share any material connected with the case on any social
media platform or with any person.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 21015 of 2026)
ASIF  APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard Mr. Siddharth Dave, learned Senior
Counsel appearing for the appellant, and Mr. Harish
Pandey,  learned  Standing  Counsel  appearing  on
advance notice for the respondent - State.
3. Considering the limited prayer made in this
appeal, we proceed to decide the appeal today
itself. Under the impugned order, the appellant’s
prayer for suspension of sentence has been rejected
by the Trial Court, which came to be preferred in a
pending appeal before the High Court wherein the
appellant has challenged his conviction by the
Trial  Court  for  committing  offences  punishable
1

## Page 295

under Sections 363 and 366 of Indian Penal Code,
1860,  sentencing  him  to  undergo  rigorous
imprisonment for 3 years and 5 years respectively.
4. According to learned senior counsel, the
appellant has already undergone 1 year and 10
months of actual sentence, and 2 years and 2 months
of total sentence including the remission.
5. Thus, out of the maximum jail sentence of 5
years, he has completed 22 months of incarceration
as noted by the High Court in the impugned order.
6. Considering that the hearing of the appeal
before  the  High  Court  may  take  time,  we  are
inclined to allow appellant’s prayer for suspension
of sentence and direct his release on bail in
connection with FIR No.669 of 2016 registered at
Police Station – Phase-3 Noida, District Gautam
Budh Nagar, for offences punishable under Sections
363 and 366 of Indian Penal Code, 1860. 
7. Accordingly, the impugned order is set aside
and the sentence imposed upon the appellant - Asif
is suspended. It is directed that the appellant
shall be released on bail pending hearing of the
appeal before the High Court, on such terms and
conditions as may be imposed by the trial court.
8. The appeal is disposed of in the above
2

## Page 296

terms.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.                OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NO.4588 OF 2026)
SHAHBAJ ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF BIHAR ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3.  Appellant  being  aggrieved  by  the  rejection  of  prayer  for  grant  of
anticipatory  bail,  is  before  this  Court  challenging  the  order  dated
15.10.2025 passed by the High Court.
4. The  case  of the  prosecution  is  that acting  on  an intel input, they
conducted a raid near Harwa Chowk District Araria and recovered large
quantity of Phensedyl Cough Syrup (T riprolidine Hydrochloride & Codeine
Phosphate Cough Syrup)  of about 4,580 liters (approx 45,800 bottles)
valued  Rs.1,03,50,800/-  from  the  pick  up  vehicle  stationed  at  the
warehouse/godwon and the persons who were loading the contraband,
also came to be arrested. The appellant who is the owner of the godown
and from where the contraband was recovered, came to be arraigned as
an accused.
1                                                                                      SLP(CRL.) NO.4588 OF 2026

## Page 299

5. We have heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties. It has
been  consistent  contention  of  the  appellant  that  he  had  leased  the
godown to a tenant by named Kakkumal Shivhare one month back prior to
incident and had produced the lease deed which had been annexed to the
petition filed before the High Court (Annexure P-1). The counter affidavit
filed  by  the  respondent  does  not  indicate  or  reflect  any  investigation
having  been  made  in  this  regard.  In  fact  the  defence  taken  by  the
appellant with regard to the premises from where the contraband was
seized, had been leased to Kakkumal Shivhare has not been controverted
in the counter affidavit and it has only been stated that they have no
comments.  As regard the complicity of the appellant in storage of the
contraband and whether the appellant was in conscious possession of the
contraband, are all issues which will have to be thrashed out after trial. As
such, we are of the considered view that the appellant is entitled for the
relief as sought for.
6. Hence, the appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside. Appellant is
ordered to be released on anticipatory bail on such terms and conditions
as the jurisdictional Investigating Officer (IO) may deem fit to impose
including the condition of directing the appellant to cooperate with the
investigation and appearing before the IO every T uesday between 10:00
am to 02:00 pm till filing of the charge-sheet and also on the condition
that appellant would appear before the trial court on all dates of hearing
except when exempted for any specific reason and shall cooperate with
the trial.
2                                                                                      SLP(CRL.) NO.4588 OF 2026

O R D E R
1. An  order  dated  18th December,  2024  passed  by  the  National  Green
Tribunal, Southern Zone, Chennai1 is under challenge in this appeal. 
2. During the pendency of the civil appeal, the State Environment Impact
Assessment Authority, State of Kerala (SEIAA) reconsidered the issue of grant of
environmental  clearance  in  favour  of  the  respondent  no.52 and  a  fresh
environmental clearance has since been granted with additional conditions. 
3. In our view, such grant of environmental clearance affords a fresh cause
of action to the appellant to approach the NGT.  
4. We grant liberty to the appellant to challenge such fresh environmental
clearance before the NGT by instituting appropriate proceedings, if so advised.
5. Since  we  are  not  examining  the  legality  and  correctness  of  the
environmental  clearance  under  challenge  before  the  NGT,  from  which  the
present appeal has arisen, or the impugned order on merits, all points are left
open for the appellant to urge before the NGT and to be contested by the
